=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s overall position

The Seller’s package materially shifts risk to Wattlebridge. The principal concern is the **combined effect** of broad disclosure, deemed buyer knowledge, restrictions applying to every type of claim, and weak completion protections. Together, these could leave the Buyer acquiring unresolved liabilities with little effective recourse.

This review is based on the Seller’s summary and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. The disclosures identify unresolved issues; they do **not** establish that those issues have been satisfactorily addressed. Seller’s descriptions of matters as “settled”, “adequate” or “ordinary-course” should not be accepted without verification.

## 1. Preserve meaningful remedies

### General warranty cap, thresholds and time limits

The proposed 20% general warranty cap is **AUD 4.8 million**. That is a commercial negotiating position, not inherently unacceptable, but its adequacy depends on the warranties, exclusions, financial diligence and Seller’s ability to pay.

The thresholds materially reduce recovery:

- Claims must **exceed AUD 25,000**; clarify treatment of related claims so one problem cannot be fragmented below the threshold.
- The **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** leaves the first AUD 250,000 with the Buyer even after the threshold is crossed.
- An **18-month notification period** may leave limited time to discover problems through post-completion reporting and audit.

**Push back:** seek a higher cap, lower de minimis and a tipping basket, under which qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Seek at least 24 months for general warranties, subject to the business’s reporting cycle.

Claim notices should require only reasonably available information, permit later quantification, and preserve properly notified claims until resolution. Check for separate, short deadlines for commencing proceedings.

### Do not apply the general regime to all claims

The proposed extension of limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to **“all Claims of any nature”** is a major issue. It could undermine specific indemnities, completion obligations, price adjustments and other negotiated protections.

**Push back:** use expressly differentiated regimes:

| Claim type | Buyer position |
|---|---|
| General warranties | Negotiated general cap, thresholds and survival period |
| Title, capacity and authority | Separate protection, ordinarily at least the full purchase price, no basket/de minimis, materially longer survival |
| Tax | Separate tax covenant/indemnity and warranties, with appropriate tax-specific limitations and survival aligned with relevant assessment periods plus a buffer |
| Known-risk indemnities | Standalone scope, cap and duration appropriate to each risk; no general basket or disclosure/knowledge defence |
| Price adjustments, repayment and completion obligations | Not restricted by general warranty limitations |
| Fraud and fraudulent concealment | Express carve-outs; preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded |

“Administrative simplicity” is not a reason to equate defective ownership of the acquired shares with an ordinary business warranty claim.

Review the actual non-reliance wording carefully. Preserve accountability for identified transaction information and negotiated warranties, fraud remedies and non-excludable statutory rights. An exclusive-remedy clause must not inadvertently prevent enforcement of completion obligations or appropriate equitable relief.

## 2. Reject blanket disclosure and constructive knowledge

The Seller seeks to disclose everything **contained or referred to** in the data room, accounts, registers and public records. Its buyer-knowledge provision goes further by excluding claims for matters merely **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers.

That approach transfers the consequences of incomplete or obscure disclosure to the Buyer. A reference to a document is not necessarily fair disclosure of a particular liability or its significance.

**Push back:**

- Require fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket disclosure of public registers and all material referred to in the data room.
- Freeze and retain an indexed copy of the disclosed data room.
- Delete constructive, imputed and “discoverable” knowledge, including blanket attribution of advisers’ knowledge. If any knowledge exclusion remains, limit it to actual knowledge of specified individuals of the relevant facts and breach.
- Ensure disclosure and buyer knowledge do not defeat specific indemnities or completion obligations.
- Refresh disclosure and diligence through signing and completion. The **22 September 2026** cutoff is historical; later developments need to be addressed without automatically qualifying warranties or waiving existing breaches.

The Disclosure Letter’s reservations do not resolve the disclosed risks. Equally, disclosure of an uncertainty should not be treated as proof that a breach or loss has occurred.

## 3. Bluefen: require an effective consent, not merely a letter

Bluefen contributes approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**. Its change-control position is therefore commercially critical.

The Seller says consent is “addressed”, but the Disclosure Letter confirms that no final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been supplied. Reasonable endeavours are not a substitute for the required outcome.

**Push back:**

- Make effective Bluefen consent a condition precedent, waivable only by the Buyer.
- Require compliance with both clauses 11.2 and 11.3, including satisfaction or effective waiver of consent conditions.
- Review the consent for fees, repricing, reduced scope, termination rights or other adverse changes.
- Require it to remain effective at completion and provide appropriate long-stop and termination rights.

Do not deem the condition satisfied merely because a document labelled “consent” is delivered.

## 4. Riverlark: discharge at completion and reconcile the price

The approximately **AUD 3.2 million** facility remains outstanding, with no final security discharge. A release promised after completion leaves the Buyer exposed to lender enforcement and change-control consequences.

**Push back:** require a verified payout statement, direct repayment through completion funds flow, and effective releases of relevant guarantees and security at completion. Any later administrative registration should be supported by binding lender undertakings and a tightly controlled process—not an unsecured Seller promise.

The debt-free/cash-free bargain also requires a clear price bridge. Confirm whether AUD 24 million is the enterprise-value reference or an already-adjusted equity price. Ensure the facility is deducted or otherwise borne by the Seller **once**, without double counting. Clarify accrued interest, break costs and discharge fees.

## 5. Completion bonuses: allocate the full cost expressly

DD-005 identifies **AUD 420,000** of conditional completion bonuses, omitted from funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the acquired company from being liable.

**Push back:**

- Verify who owes each bonus, when it becomes payable and the continued-employment conditions.
- Allocate transaction-triggered bonuses to the Seller through an express price deduction, debt-like item or Seller-funded payment mechanism.
- Include applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other employer on-costs.
- Reconcile payment, withholding and payroll evidence.

If liabilities remain contingent beyond completion, use a suitable retention or indemnity. Avoid counting the same amount in both debt and working capital.

## 6. Ironquay IP: payment alone may not secure ownership

The disclosed clause conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The **AUD 180,000** open balance is a warning, but is not independently verified proof of non-payment.

A payment-only indemnity may not cover the real risk: missing ownership or usage rights, infringement exposure, remediation costs or interruption to a core product.

**Push back:**

- Verify the payment position, full SOW3 fees and contractual ownership/licensing terms.
- Require evidence of cleared payment and an effective confirmatory assignment or other necessary rights documentation.
- Check the chain of title, subcontractor rights, background IP and third-party components.
- Expand the indemnity to cover losses from the identified rights defect, not merely the outstanding invoice.

If the materials are essential to the business, satisfactory rights should be a completion requirement. General IP warranty protection should remain substantive rather than being treated as “settled”.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate without prejudging the result

The known fact is delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address, potentially involving about **1,240 records**. Access, scope and notification requirements remain uncertain. It is neither established as immaterial nor established as a notifiable breach.

**Push back:**

- Obtain preservation of evidence and a documented investigation into access, downloads, link security, data content and containment.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual and other notification duties promptly, including whether Australian eligible-data-breach requirements apply.
- Require appropriate remediation and updates before completion.
- Seek a tailored indemnity for the pre-completion incident, covering investigation, remediation and legally recoverable resulting liabilities.

Ensure disclosure does not eliminate that indemnity. If diligence reveals material exposure, consider a retention or completion condition proportionate to the findings.

## 8. Supplier renewals: assess the substance and aggregate commitment

Three related **AUD 110,000** renewals total **AUD 330,000**. They should be assessed together. The disclosures do not establish that they are unavoidable, ordinary-course, accrued or terminable.

Review timing, scope, authority, termination rights, prepayments and whether they overlap existing services. Determine their treatment under the agreed accounting definitions.

**Push back:** impose appropriate pre-completion controls on material commitments and address any exceptional or unauthorised cost through price treatment or specific protection. Do **not** automatically classify all future operating expenditure as debt.

## 9. Title, lease and Mossvale: verify, without inventing consent requirements

**Share title:** DD-012 is evidence of registered ownership, not a complete title investigation. Verify the issued capital, valid issue and ownership, options and convertible rights, transfer restrictions, encumbrances and corporate approvals. Obtain effective transfer documents and releases at completion, supported by unqualified title warranties under the separate fundamental regime.

**Office lease:** the disclosed requirement is notification, not landlord consent. Verify the actual lease and require the necessary notice and evidence of compliance.

**Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not necessarily apply to a share sale. Review the complete agreement for change-control, deemed-assignment and termination provisions. Do not demand unnecessary consent solely because an assignment clause exists.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Completion certainty:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/security releases, verified share title and any business-critical Ironquay rights.
2. **Protect the economics:** reconcile the AUD 24 million price, debt treatment, bonuses and on-costs, without double counting.
3. **Preserve recourse:** reject all-claims limitations, blanket disclosure and constructive buyer knowledge; separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity protections.
4. **Resolve known risks:** investigate the export incident and supplier commitments; secure targeted remediation and financial protection.
5. **Make recovery practical:** assess Harbourglass’s post-completion resources and negotiate retention, escrow or other security where appropriate.

**Bottom line:** neither disclosure nor a promise to deal with matters after completion delivers the debt-free/cash-free, legally owned and operationally secure business the Buyer is paying for. Resolve essential matters before or at completion, and allocate residual risks expressly rather than leaving them inside a weakened general warranty regime.
